title: Tries
summary: Store many strings in a shared prefix tree so prefix questions cost time proportional to the query, not the dictionary.
lesson:
How it works
- A trie node holds one child per possible next character and a flag that marks where a stored word ends.
- Inserting or looking up a word walks one node per character, so each operation is `O(L)` for a word of length `L`, regardless of how many words are stored.
- Words that share a prefix share the path for that prefix, which is what makes prefix queries cheap.

When to reach for it
- You answer many queries about prefixes, autocomplete, or which stored words start with some text.
- You search for many words at once and want to share the work for their common prefixes.
- Characters come from a small fixed alphabet, so children fit in an array.

Common patterns
- Array children (`new Node[26]`) for lowercase letters; a map when the alphabet is large or unknown.
- End-of-word flag versus "any word passes through here": they answer different questions.
- Wildcard matching: when a pattern character can match anything, try every child and succeed if any branch matches.
- Pairing a trie with depth-first search over another structure, pruning as soon as the current path is not a prefix of any word.

Pitfalls
- Treating "the path exists" as "the word exists"; a stored prefix is not a stored word.
- Reporting the same found word twice; clear its end marker or deduplicate once it is reported.
- Memory: a node per character with a full child array adds up, so share prefixes and prune empty branches when the set changes.
